headline: Massachusetts reports record September for battery fires as safety week begins
dek: State fire officials say local departments logged 22 battery fires last month, twice the year-earlier total, as Massachusetts urges safer charging during Fire Prevention Week.
body: Massachusetts fire departments reported 22 battery fires in September, the highest monthly total since the state began tracking the incidents, State Fire Marshal Jon M. Davine said Monday. The figure was double the number reported a year earlier, according to the Massachusetts Department of Fire Services, which released the data as Gov. Maura Healey declared Oct. 4-10 Fire Prevention Week.

The new count gives a statewide measure to a hazard that is increasingly part of ordinary household life. Lithium-ion batteries power phones, laptops, earbuds, power tools, e-bikes, scooters and other rechargeable devices. The Department of Fire Services says damaged batteries or improper charging can cause overheating, fire or explosions. The department's [Fire Prevention Week announcement](https://www.mass.gov/news/governor-healey-declares-october-4-10-fire-prevention-week) does not identify the individual September fires, their causes, the number of injuries or the amount of property damage, so the monthly total should not be read as a measure of severity.

The September result also arrives after a warning from fire officials across New England. The [Boston Globe reported](https://www.bostonglobe.com/2026/09/25/metro/big-e-fairgoers-fire-safety-tips/) that fire marshals from Massachusetts, Connecticut, New Hampshire and Vermont used a Big E appearance in West Springfield to emphasize safe charging and working smoke alarms. The Globe reported that Massachusetts battery fires had risen from fewer than 20 to more than 130 in a few years and quoted Davine saying the state was on track for a record month. The newer state announcement supplies the final September count.

For residents, the advice is specific: use the cord and charger supplied with a device or one approved by its manufacturer; charge on a hard, flat surface rather than a bed, couch or pillow; and unplug the device when it is fully charged. The [Concord Fire Department](https://concordfirenews.com/2026/10/01/national-fire-prevention-week-is-october-4-10-steps-to-charge-devices-safely/) separately advises charging while awake and nearby, keeping larger devices outside when possible, and never blocking an exit with an e-bike, scooter or power tool.

Officials also want people to recognize signs of a failing battery. A device that becomes unusually hot, swells, smokes or develops a strange smell should no longer be used, the state says. Residents should leave and call 911 if a device catches fire. The Massachusetts guidance says used batteries do not belong in household trash or recycling, where they can be crushed or damaged in collection and transfer equipment; instead, residents should use a household hazardous-waste event or a battery-recycling location.

The risks extend beyond homes. The [National Park Service](https://www.nps.gov/articles/000/nps-structural-fire-program-observes-fire-prevention-week-2026.htm), which is observing the same Oct. 4-10 week, documented 2026 battery incidents involving a boat at Glen Canyon National Recreation Area, an audio-tour player at Alcatraz and an e-bike at Grand Canyon National Park. Those examples are outside New England and do not establish a Massachusetts trend, but they illustrate why agencies are focusing on charging practices rather than only on a particular product category.

Fire Prevention Week is a public-education observance, not a new Massachusetts restriction on rechargeable devices. The 2026 theme is “Charge into Fire Safety: Safe Charging Is a Superpower,” coordinated nationally by the National Fire Protection Association. Massachusetts officials say residents should look for recognized safety certification marks such as UL or Intertek/ETL when buying devices, keep large battery-powered equipment away from doors and stairs, and make sure smoke alarms can be heard wherever people sleep.

The immediate takeaway is practical, while important questions remain open. The state has not published a September incident list in the announcement, and the release does not say how many fires involved e-bikes, scooters, chargers or other equipment. Those details would help explain the record month. For now, fire officials are using the available statewide count and the start of Fire Prevention Week to push habits that can reduce heat, overcharging and blocked escape routes before a battery problem becomes a structure fire.
author: NorthEast News Desk
